penalties_summary: The report establishes no new fines or statutory penalties; non-compliance with human-authorship standards or AI-material disclosure rules results in refusal, limitation, or cancellation of copyright registration under Title 17 (preventing enforcement of exclusive rights in court or eligibility for statutory blanket royalty pools such as the Mechanical Licensing Collective).
implementation_notes: Part 2 of the U.S. Copyright Office's multi-part report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, released January 29, 2025 following the August 2023 Notice of Inquiry (over 10,000 public comments). Reaffirms that U.S. copyright requires human authorship under the Copyright Clause and Title 17, distinguishes assistive AI uses (fully protectable) from generative AI outputs lacking sufficient human expressive control, concludes that prompts alone—even detailed or iteratively revised prompts—do not confer authorship under current technology, confirms protection for perceptible human expressive inputs and creative selection/arrangement/modification of AI outputs on a case-by-case basis, surveys international approaches (South Korea, Japan, China, EU, UK, Canada, Australia), and rejects creating new copyright or sui generis protection for purely AI-generated works. To be operationalized via updated registration guidance and revisions to the Compendium of U.S. Copyright Office Practices.
